sorona.origin: Sorona is a brand of Covation Biomaterials LLC, based near Newark, Delaware, which is owned by China's Huafon Group. DuPont commercialized Sorona in 2000 and sold its biomaterials business to Huafon in a deal announced in 2020 and closed in 2022. The generic fiber is poly(trimethylene terephthalate), PTT, a polyester. Covation states that Sorona is 37% bio-based by weight, from 1,3-propanediol (PDO) produced by fermenting corn sugar; the terephthalic acid portion is petroleum-derived.
sorona.structure: PTT is an aromatic polyester formed from terephthalic acid (or its dimethyl ester) and 1,3-propanediol, a three-carbon diol, whereas PET uses two-carbon ethylene glycol. The odd number of methylene groups makes the chain adopt a helical, zigzag conformation in the crystal, so the molecule can extend and recover like a spring at small strains. PTT has a melting point of about 228 C and a glass transition of about 45 C, both lower than PET, and a lower initial modulus, which accounts for its softer hand.
sorona.process: Covation describes a two-part supply chain. Bio-PDO is made by fermenting glucose from corn with an engineered microorganism, then purified; its main plant at Loudon, Tennessee, is a joint venture. The PDO is polymerized with terephthalic acid by melt polycondensation to PTT at Kinston, North Carolina. The polymer is sold as chip to fiber makers, who melt-spin, draw and texture it into filament yarn or bicomponent stretch yarns, or cut it into staple and carpet fiber.
sorona.performance: PTT fibers show good elastic recovery at low extensions, better than PET and similar to nylon in published data, which gives mechanical stretch without elastane in some constructions. The lower glass transition allows disperse dyeing at lower temperatures than PET, often without carriers. Moisture regain is low, as for other polyesters, and PTT carpet fiber is marketed for stain resistance. It is thermoplastic and melts. Covation's life-cycle comparisons against nylon 6 are producer claims.
sorona.identify: Burn behavior resembles polyester (melts, drips, sooty smoke, hard bead); burn tests are indicative only. FTIR identifies a terephthalate polyester, and differential scanning calorimetry separates PTT (melting about 228 C) from PET (about 250 to 260 C). Radiocarbon analysis could detect the bio-based carbon share. Sorona is often misdescribed as elastane or as a plant fiber; it is a partly bio-based synthetic polyester.
sorona.labeling: Sorona is a trademark, not a generic name. In the US, 16 CFR 303.7(c) allows triexta as an alternative generic name for a polyester subclass in which at least 90 mole percent of the glycol is 1,3-propanediol; the FTC adopted it in 2009 on a petition from Mohawk, DuPont and PTT Poly Canada. Polyester is also permitted. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 has no separate PTT name, so polyester applies. Bio-based content claims need substantiation.
sorona.past: PTT was known in polymer chemistry for decades but was costly because 1,3-propanediol was expensive. DuPont and partners developed a corn-sugar fermentation route to PDO, allowing DuPont to commercialize Sorona in 2000 and later scale bio-PDO at Loudon. In 2009 the FTC created the triexta subclass, reflecting carpet makers' interest in PTT. In 2020 DuPont agreed to sell its biomaterials unit to Huafon Group for about 240 million dollars; the deal closed in 2022 and the business was relaunched as Covation Biomaterials, which marked Sorona's 25th anniversary in 2025.
facts: Polyester, PTT subclass (US alternative name triexta)

bemberg.origin: Bemberg is the cupro fiber brand of Asahi Kasei Corporation of Japan, produced at its plant in Nobeoka, Miyazaki Prefecture, since 1931. The generic fiber is cupro: regenerated cellulose made by the cuprammonium process. Its feedstock is cotton linter, the short fuzz left on cottonseed after ginning and a by-product of cottonseed-oil processing. Asahi Kasei presents its Bemberg operation as a rare, possibly sole, commercial source of cupro, which buyers can confirm with the producer.
bemberg.structure: Cupro is regenerated cellulose (cellulose II), chemically the same polymer as viscose and lyocell, but its filaments can be made very fine and its cross-section is nearly round and smooth, without the serrated skin of viscose. Cotton linter pulp provides cellulose of high purity. Stretch spinning draws the filaments while they are still plastic, giving fine deniers and a uniform, lustrous surface that suits linings and fluid woven fabrics.
bemberg.process: In outline, purified cotton linter is dissolved in a cuprammonium solution, an aqueous complex of copper(II) ions and ammonia that dissolves cellulose directly. The solution is filtered and extruded through spinnerets into flowing water that stretches the coagulating filaments (the stretch-spinning method associated with Bemberg), and the fiber is then treated with acid to remove copper and complete regeneration. Figures on copper and ammonia recovery should be taken from the producer's own sustainability information rather than assumed.
bemberg.performance: Cupro is highly absorbent and, like other regenerated cellulose, loses strength when wet, so gentle handling matters. Its smooth, round filaments give low friction and good slip in linings, and the fiber dissipates static better than synthetic lining yarns because it holds moisture. It chars rather than melts, and dyes with reactive and direct dyes. Comfort and sustainability attributes in Asahi Kasei's marketing are producer statements whose test conditions should be checked.
bemberg.identify: Burn tests (indicative only) show cellulose behavior: fast burning, afterglow, paper-like odor, soft grey ash. Under the microscope cupro shows smooth, fine filaments with a round cross-section and no striations, which helps distinguish it from viscose. FTIR confirms cellulose but not the process. Cupro is often confused with silk or sold under the loose term 'Bemberg lining' for any smooth lining.
bemberg.labeling: Bemberg is a trademark, not a generic name. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 lists cupro as a fiber name for cellulose regenerated by the cuprammonium process. In the US, the FTC generic names at 16 CFR 303.7 do not list cupro separately; regenerated cellulose falls under rayon, so US labels generally use rayon. The trademark may appear only alongside the generic name.
bemberg.past: The German company J. P. Bemberg began commercial production of artificial textile fiber by the cuprammonium process in 1897. In 1901 Edmund Thiele developed a stretch-spinning system for the firm, which from 1908 sold fine-filament artificial silk under the Bemberg name. Asahi Kasei took up this technology and scaled it to commercial production at its Bemberg plant in Nobeoka in 1931. Over the following decades the Bemberg name became closely identified with cupro itself, especially in fine suit and coat linings, which is why the trademark is often misused as a generic term.
facts: developed by Edmund Thiele for J. P. Bemberg, 1901
